fsis.statement: Reheat leftovers to 165 F. Cook all poultry to a safe minimum internal temperature of 165 F as measured with a food thermometer.
fsis.note: USDA FSIS fact sheet 'Cooking Safely in the Microwave Oven', revised June 2011 (GPO archived copy). 165 F = 74 C.

fsis.statement: Do not use foam trays and plastic wraps because they are not heat stable at high temperatures.
Only use cookware that is specially manufactured for use in the microwave oven.
Plastic storage containers such as margarine tubs, take-out containers, whipped topping bowls should not be used in the microwave; these containers can warp or melt.
fsis.note: Paraphrase joining two quoted fragments. The exact phrase 'cold storage containers' was NOT found in this version.

fsis.statement: Do not let plastic wrap touch foods during microwaving.
Always allow standing time, which completes the cooking, before checking the internal temperature with a food thermometer.
Cooking times may vary because ovens vary in power and efficiency.
fsis.note: This version does not explicitly say 'follow package directions'.

fsis.statement: NRTE breaded stuffed chicken product labels typically instruct consumers to cook the product in an oven, and the label specifically warns against the use of a microwave.
fsis.note: FSIS final determination, Federal Register 89(85), May 1, 2024, docket FSIS-2022-0013 (Salmonella adulterant in NRTE breaded stuffed chicken). Describes label content; FSIS itself does not issue a blanket microwave ban.

fsis.statement: FSIS-requested label statement: 'Uncooked: For Safety, Must be Cooked to an Internal Temperature of 165 degrees F as Measured by Use of a Thermometer.'
fsis.note: Requested after 2006 outbreaks. Same notice: most case patients in 1998 and 2005-2006 outbreaks used a microwave.

fsis.statement: Raw breaded stuffed chicken products are pre-browned and may appear cooked, but the chicken is raw; they are typically cooked from frozen, increasing the risk of not reaching the temperature needed to destroy Salmonella.

Packaging instructs consumers to cook these products in ovens; 29% of surveyed consumers used microwaves; 8% used a microwave of <=750 W, which might be insufficient to thoroughly cook such products; microwaves require adjusting cooking times based on wattage.
fsis.note: Marshall KE et al. MMWR 2022;71:1511-1516, doi:10.15585/mmwr.mm7148a2 (CDC, not FSIS; erratum published, check current version).

wattage_conversion.statement: It is important to know the wattage of your oven in order to adjust cooking times. Wattage is on the inside of the door, the serial number plate on the back, or in the owner's manual.
wattage_conversion.note: Conagra Brands (frozen meal manufacturer). No conversion table or formula given.

wattage_conversion.statement: Microwave ovens that are 700 watts or lower will only heat, not cook, your food.

Time-to-boil test (attributed to USDA): 1 cup ice-cold water in 2-cup glass measure, HIGH up to 4 min. Boils <2 min = 1000 W or higher; 2.5 min = about 800 W or higher; 3 min = 650-700 W or higher; >3 min or not by 4 min = 300-500 W.
wattage_conversion.note: Original USDA document for this test not fetched.

wattage_conversion.statement: Microwaves require adjusting cooking times based on the microwave's wattage.

UK labeling scheme: food makers give heating times by oven class (e.g., 'if you have an A oven heat for x minutes, C oven = y minutes'); British output procedure uses both 1000 g and 350 g water loads.
wattage_conversion.note: IMPI newsletter The Wave, Jan/Feb 2017, President's Message (R. Schiffmann).

wattage_conversion.statement: Production ovens disperse at least +/-15% around the mean; an oven sold as 1000 W could be 850-1150 W; author never found an oven above its claimed 1000 W. The 1000 g water test poorly represents 10-12 oz meals (water equivalency 200-400 g) because of load factor.
wattage_conversion.note: Expert opinion in a professional society newsletter, not peer-reviewed.

wattage_conversion.statement: IEC 60705-2006 is the current IEC microwave oven test standard (replacing IEC 705); DOE-tested units had rated output 700-1300 W.
IEC 60705 output-power test details (1000 g water, ~10 C start, ~10 K rise, formula with container correction)
wattage_conversion.note: Standard is paywalled; procedure numbers not confirmed. URL is the official preview only.

wattage_conversion.statement: Panasonic service check (simplified, not IEC): 1 L tap water, HIGH exactly 1 min; minimum temperature rise 8.6 C for a 1000 W unit and 9.4 C for 1100 W.
Cook time inversely proportional to wattage: t2 = t1 x (P1 / P2)
wattage_conversion.note: Only found on calculator websites (not authoritative). It follows from a simple energy balance Q = P_abs x t if absorbed power scales with rated power, but IMPI notes load-dependent coupling and +/-15% unit dispersion, so treat as a first-order approximation.

food_thermal.note: Schwartzberg H, Singh RP, Sarkar A. 'Freezing and thawing of foods: computation methods and thermal properties correlation', ch. 3 in Heat Transfer in Food Processing, WIT Transactions on State of the Art in Science and Engineering vol 13, WIT Press, 2007.

food_thermal.property: latent heat of fusion of water at 273.16 K
food_thermal.note: 143.4 BTU/lb. Temperature-corrected form dH_av = dH_0 + 0.5 (C_I - C_w)(T_0 - T).

food_thermal.value: C_F = n_s C_s + (n_wo - B n_s) C_I + B n_s C_w; effective C below initial freezing point T_i: C = C_F + (n_wo - B n_s)(T_0 - T_i) dH_0 / (T_0 - T)^2
food_thermal.note: n_wo initial water mass fraction, n_s solute fraction, B bound-water parameter. Useful for modelling the thawing plateau.

food_thermal.property: example food inputs used in worked example (not typical values)
food_thermal.note: Authors present these as illustrative inputs only.

food_thermal.property: specific heat, chicken (broilers) above / below freezing
food_thermal.note: Also: beef round 3.10/1.59, carrots 3.81/1.84, potato 3.43/1.72. Page cites no primary source.

food_thermal.property: specific heat of typical prepared/frozen meals 3.5-3.8 kJ/(kg K) (unfrozen)
food_thermal.note: Plausible from water content, but no fetched source states it for prepared meals. ASHRAE Refrigeration Handbook 'Thermal Properties of Foods' chapter (Choi-Okos) was not accessible.
Recommend pulling per-product water (g/100 g) from USDA FoodData Central for each entree type.

microwave_efficiency.statement: Panasonic acceptance criterion implies about 600 W absorbed by 1 L water in 60 s for a 1000 W-rated oven (about 60% of rating), and about 656 W for 1100 W (about 60%).
microwave_efficiency.note: 1000 g x 4.187 J/(g K) x 8.6 K / 60 s = 600 W. This is a minimum pass threshold of a simplified field check (ignores beaker heat capacity and losses), not a measured mean efficiency.

microwave_efficiency.statement: Absorbed power in 1 L water (Pmax) measured in four domestic ovens: 850 W-rated 897.7 W; 650 W-rated 674.2 W; 900 W-rated 880.2 W; 650 W-rated 684.7 W.
microwave_efficiency.note: Housova J, Hoke K. Czech J Food Sci 2002;20(3):117-124. Ratio is our calculation. The paper's text also cites 882.4 W for the 850 W oven. Shows rated output approximates power absorbed by a large (1 L) water load, not by a small meal.

microwave_efficiency.statement: Small food loads (10-12 oz meals, water equivalency 200-400 g) receive a different power than the 1000 g test load because of load factor.
Fraction of rated power absorbed by small (~300 g) food loads is 50-70%
microwave_efficiency.note: No fetched source gave this range. Recommend measuring with the app's own calibration (e.g., 300 g water, timed rise) or treating as a user-tunable parameter.

container_geometry.note: Case of 75 = 9.23 lb net; 9.23 lb x 453.6 g/lb / 75 = 55.8 g per tray.
Pack of 80 = 11,173 g; 11,173 / 80 = 139.7 g, upper bound since pack weight may include carton. Foodservice size, not single-serve.

container_geometry.item: CPET single-serve tray wall thickness 0.3-0.8 mm
PP microwave cup wall thickness 0.3-0.6 mm
Inner food-contact area for ~300 g meal

notes: The live FSIS page https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/food-safety-basics/microwave-ovens-and-food-safety could not be fetched (proxy 403). FSIS microwave statements are cited from the GPO-archived FSIS fact sheet (rev. June 2011). Re-check wording against the live FSIS page before citing in the app.

FSIS does not issue a general rule that NRTE stuffed chicken must never be microwaved; the 2024 Federal Register notice reports that product labels typically instruct oven cooking and warn against microwaves, and that most outbreak cases involved microwave cooking.
No USDA/FSIS conversion table for wattage was found. The inverse-proportional time rule is UNVERIFIED and is only a first-order approximation.

Rated microwave output is defined by a large water load (IEC 60705, ~1000 g); absorbed power for small meal loads differs (IMPI 2017). Houssova & Hoke 2002 show absorbed power in 1 L water close to the rating; the Panasonic field check threshold implies about 60% for a 1 L/1 min test.

Polymer temperature limits differ by source and grade; designerdata.nl and Wikipedia are SECONDARY and contain internal inconsistencies (noted per entry). Prefer the container maker's stated range when a product is known.
Inline Plastics' table labels its SG 1.33 row 'Polyethylene'; its assignment to PET is our inference.
